# Irritable bowel syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Irritable bowel syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/XS09y2)

---

## Summary

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic condition that is very common in North America and Europe. It is thought that the underlying pathophysiology involves changes in gastrointestinal motility, <u>visceral</u> hypersensitivity, and altered gastrointestinal permeability. Patients present with <u>recurrent abdominal pain</u> associated with changes in stool frequency, form, and/or appearance. IBS is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on the <u>Rome IV criteria for IBS</u> and ruling out alternative diagnoses. Nonpharmacological treatment includes dietary modifications (e.g., avoidance of trigger foods) and psychobehavioral therapies. Pharmacological therapies such as <u>loperamide</u>, <u>laxatives</u>, and <u>lubiprostone</u> are targeted to <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>constipation</u>, and <u>global</u> IBS symptoms, respectively.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 10–20% in North America and Europe (accounts for 20–50% of referrals to gastroenterologists)

* Sex: : In Western countries, women are 1.5–2 times more likely to be affected than men.

* Age: highest <u>prevalence</u> in individuals aged 20–39 [[1]](/library/YOanIk)

* Associated conditions [[2]](/library/Cu1qti0)

* <u>Soma</u><u>tic</u> pain syndromes: <u>fibromyalgia</u>, <u>chronic fatigue syndrome</u>, <u>functional chest pain</u>

* Psychiatric disorders: <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>anxiety disorder</u>, <u>somatization disorder</u>

* Gastrointestinal disorders: <u>GERD</u>, <u>functional dyspepsia</u>





References:[[1]](/library/YOanIk)[[3]](/library/cOaark)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder without a specific organic cause. The pathophysiological processes leading to IBS are multifaceted and not yet fully understood. The most common findings associated with IBS are:




* Altered gastrointestinal motility

* <u>Visceral</u> hypersensitivity/<u>hyperalgesia</u>

* Altered permeability of the gastrointestinal <u>mucosa</u>

* Psychosocial aspects





References:[[4]](/library/dOaork)[[5]](/library/VOaGrk)

---

## Clinical features

IBS is characterized by <u>chronic abdominal pain</u> and changes in bowel habits (see also “<u>Rome IV criteria for IBS</u>”).




* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Frequency, intensity, and localization generally vary widely from patient to patient

* Typically related to defecation

* Altered bowel habits: : <u>diarrhea</u> and/or <u>constipation</u>

* Other gastrointestinal symptoms

* <u>Nausea</u>, reflux, early satiety

* Passing of mucus, abdominal <u>bloating</u>

* Extraintestinal symptoms

* Generalized somatic symptoms (e.g., <u>pain</u> or fatigue, as in <u>fibromyalgia</u>)

* Disturbed sexual function

* <u>Dysmenorrhea</u>

* Increased <u>urinary frequency</u> and urgency

* <u>Physical examination</u>: normal

---

## Classification

Several subtypes of IBS exist and are defined by stool quality.  [[6]](/library/KK1Uh30)




* IBS-D: <u>diarrhea</u> is the predominant symptom

* IBS-C: <u>constipation</u> is the predominant symptom

* IBS‑M: mixed <u>diarrhea</u> and <u>constipation</u>

* IBS-U: <u>criteria for IBS</u> are met but bowel movements can't be categorized into the above subgroups

---

## Diagnosis

IBS is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> (using the <u>Rome IV criteria for IBS</u>). Limited diagnostic studies are recommended for the primary purpose of ruling out alternative diagnoses.




### Approach [[6]](/library/KK1Uh30)




* Evaluate for <u>diagnostic criteria for IBS</u>.

* Screen for <u>red flag symptoms</u> (see “Differential diagnoses”).

* Obtain a limited diagnostic workup to rule out alternative diagnoses.





> [!TIP]
> An acute change in bowel habits, <u>signs of overt GI bleeding</u>, or other <u>red flags for CRC</u> should prompt further diagnostic evaluation.




### Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome [[7]](/library/EtY82I)




All of the following criteria must be met to diagnose IBS.




* Timing: ≥ 6 months since the onset of symptoms

* Symptoms

* <u>Recurrent abdominal pain</u> (≥ 1 day per week during the previous 3 months)

* PLUS ≥ 2 of the following

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> related to defecation

* Change in stool frequency

* Change in appearance of stool





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[6]](/library/KK1Uh30)[[8]](/library/6K1jh30)




The following studies should routinely be considered to rule out alternative etiologies :




* All patients: <u>CBC</u> (<u>anemia</u> requires further evaluation)

* In patients with <u>diarrhea</u>

* <u>Fecal calprotectin</u> and <u>CRP</u>

* <u>Celiac disease serology</u>

* Stool testing for <u>giardiasis</u> [[9]](/library/tMcXq10)

* In patients with relevant symptoms and history

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for infectious gastroenteritis</u>





### <u>Colonoscopy</u> [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)



* Only recommended in patients:

* With <u>red flags for CRC</u>

* Due for age-appropriate <u>screening for CRC</u>  [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)

---

## Differential diagnoses

| Overview of common differential diagnoses |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Condition | General appearance | <u>Pain</u> | Stool habits |
| Irritable bowel syndrome | <br>* Healthy; no weight loss<br><br> | <br>* Alleviated by defecation; diffuse; no nighttime <u>pain</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Diarrhea</u> or <u>constipation</u>, possibly alternating; no blood; no nighttime <u>diarrhea</u><br><br> |
| <u>Crohn disease</u> | <br>* Weight loss; <u>malnourishment</u><br><br> | <br>* Usually constant; occurs particularly in the right lower abdomen; may appear at night<br><br> | <br>* Non‑bloody, <u>watery diarrhea</u>; increased frequency; possible nighttime <u>diarrhea</u><br><br> |
| <u>Ulcerative colitis</u> | <br>* Weight loss only in severe cases<br><br> | <br>* Mostly left lower abdomen; may occur at night<br><br> | <br>* Bloody <u>diarrhea</u> with mucus<br><br> |
| <u>Colorectal carcinoma</u> | <br>* Weight loss<br><br> | <br>* Often no <u>pain</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Right-sided <u>carcinomas</u>: <u>melena</u>, <u>diarrhea</u><br><br>* Left-sided <u>carcinomas</u>: <u>constipation</u><br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Red flag symptoms</u>: nighttime <u>diarrhea</u> and abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, bloody stools, weight loss, and acute onset of symptoms.




### Other differential diagnoses to consider




* Bacterial or <u>viral gastroenteritis</u>

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u>/<u>hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Celiac disease</u>

* <u>Lactose intolerance</u>

* Bacterial overgrowth syndrome (i.e., <u>SIBO</u>)

* See also: “<u>Differential diagnoses of acute abdominal pain</u>”

* See also: “<u>Causes of chronic diarrhea</u>”

* See also: “<u>Causes of constipation</u>”





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

Currently, there are no curative treatments for IBS. Management is focused on treating the associated symptoms.




### Nonpharmacological treatment [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)




* Dietary adjustments

* Soluble fiber supplements (e.g., <u>psyllium</u>)  [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)

* Avoidance of trigger foods (e.g., trial of <u>elimination diet</u>)

* Low FODMAP diet: diet low in fermentable oligosaccharides, <u>disaccharides</u>, <u>monosaccharides</u>, and polyols

* Consider the support of a registered dietitian.

* Lifestyle changes [[6]](/library/KK1Uh30)

* <u>Regular physical activity</u>

* <u>Stress</u> management (e.g., relaxation techniques)

* Psychobehavioral therapy [[6]](/library/KK1Uh30)

* <u>Patient-centered care</u>, strong <u>therapeutic alliance</u>

* Gut-directed <u>psychotherapy</u> (i.e., <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> and hypnotherapy)

* Adjunctive therapy: peppermint oil for <u>global</u> symptom relief [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)[[10]](/library/Mq1M_30)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Elimination diets</u> that restrict fermentable oligosaccharides, <u>disaccharides</u>, <u>monosaccharides</u>, and polyols (i.e., a <u>low FODMAP diet</u>) should be undertaken with the support of a registered dietitian in order to avoid nutritional deficiencies. [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)




### Pharmacotherapy [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)




* Evidence for pharmacological therapy is mixed and recommendations vary between guidelines.

* Consult a specialist for refractory symptoms and/or long-term treatment.





#### <u>Diarrhea</u> [[11]](/library/K61UN30)




* <u>Loperamide</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Rifaximin</u> DOSAGE

* Alternative medications: include <u>alosetron</u> (a selective <u>5-HT3 receptor antagonist</u>), <u>eluxadoline</u> (<u>opioid</u> <u>agonist</u>/<u>antagonist</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> When treating IBS-associated <u>diarrhea</u>, use caution to avoid <u>constipation</u> as an adverse effect, especially in patients with IBS-M or IBS-U.




#### <u>Constipation</u> [[12]](/library/661jN30)




* <u>Polyethylene glycol</u> (<u>PEG</u>) DOSAGE    [[11]](/library/K61UN30)[[12]](/library/661jN30)

* Alternative medications:

* <u>Intestinal secretagogues</u>

* <u>Tenapanor</u>

* A <u>sodium-hydrogen antiporter</u> 3 inhibitor

* Increases water secretion into the intestinal lumen and has antinociceptive effects.

* <u>Tegaserod</u>: a partial 5-HT<sub>4</sub> <u>receptor</u> <u>agonist</u>





#### Abdominal <u>pain</u> [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)[[11]](/library/K61UN30)[[12]](/library/661jN30)




The following can be considered to treat associated abdominal <u>pain</u>:




* <u>Antispasmodics</u>: e.g., <u>dicyclomine</u>, hyoscyamine

* <u>Tricyclic antidepressants</u>: e.g., <u>amitriptyline</u> DOSAGE (<u>off-label</u>) [[8]](/library/6K1jh30)





### Disposition [[13]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* IBS may be managed in an outpatient setting; arrange for close follow-up.

* Provide patients with <u>return precautions</u> if <u>alarm features</u> develop (see “Clinical features”).
